How it works

Understanding Energy Pricing

You pay for the GPU energy each request actually consumes — not an arbitrary per-token markup. For efficient models that can mean paying a fraction of token-priced rates.

Two ways to pay

Token pricing vs. energy pricing, in plain English

Both are just ways of charging for the same request. The difference is what you're billed for — words, or the actual power the GPU burns to produce them.

Token pricing

You pay a set price for every token (roughly a word-piece) that goes in and comes out. The price is fixed per model and set by the provider — it doesn't change with how hard the model actually had to work.

You're billed for
Words in & words out
How we do it

Energy pricing

You pay for the energy the GPU actually uses, metered per request at one flat rate for every model. An efficient model that does the same job with less compute simply costs you less — so for efficient (MoE) models this is often dramatically cheaper.

You're billed for
Actual energy used (kWh)

The rest of this page explains exactly how energy pricing works and shows the live average energy each model uses, measured from real traffic.

What energy pricing is

Every request you send runs on a GPU and consumes a measurable amount of energy. We meter that energy per request and bill it at a flat rate (currently $10.00/kWh on pay-as-you-go), the same rate for every model. Token pricing, by contrast, charges a per-token price that each provider sets independently of how much compute the model actually uses.

Because the rate is the same across models, energy pricing rewards efficiency directly: a model that does the same work with less compute simply costs you less.

How energy scales with your request

Request size

Energy grows with the work done. A long generation that streams thousands of output tokens consumes far more energy than a one-line classification call. Output tokens cost more energy than input tokens because each one is generated sequentially through the full model.

Cache hits

When a prefix of your prompt is already cached on the server, those tokens don't have to be recomputed. Higher cache-hit ratios — common with long shared system prompts or multi-turn agents — mean less energy per request and lower cost.

Because real requests vary by orders of magnitude, a single number can't honestly describe a model's energy. Instead we publish the average measured energy per request at each request size over the trailing 7 days of real usage — a grid you can read off for your own size of request. A model publishes its numbers once we've measured at least 1,000 real requests in that window.

How to read the board. Right now pools ALL request sizes mixed together over the latest hour, while 7-day typical covers typical-size requests only — different bases, so those numbers legitimately differ. The vs 7-day meter and label compare this hour against the model's own 7-day pooled average. The 48h trend shows per-hour pooled energy around that average (the dashed line in taller views) — recent movement around the baseline, not a restatement of it. Where shown, a dotted blue line marks the token-price equivalent and an amber dash-dot line marks the Surge Protection ceiling. Energy scales with request size; per-size figures are in the grid below.

Average over the last 7 days of real usage. Columns are prompt-size bands (input tokens). Energy depends more on how long a request holds the GPU than on how many tokens it has — so what you pay reflects real GPU work, not token count.
